translation.english_title: Do not look at the rain of my two eyes

english_lines: Do not look at the rain of my two eyes,
Look instead at my heart rejoicing,
My son Ponmudi, bearing the battle-sword,
Struck down the base men and gave up his life,
Struck down the base men and gave up his life,
(My two eyes).
notes: The source's two differently spaced `உயிர்துறந்தான் / உயிர் துறந்தான்` lines remain two repeated English lines rather than being collapsed.
The mother holds grief and pride together; the English does not turn the opening into a purely mournful elegy.

english_lines: Saying love must not be forbidden — I joined to him,
A casket of sculpted beauty as his companion —
A maiden young-deer suited to his thought,
I waited to marry them after he returned from the field.
notes: `கட்டழகுப் பெட்டகம்` remains a concrete `casket of sculpted beauty`, and `கன்னி இளமானை` remains `maiden young-deer`; the images are not generalized into `beautiful bride`.

english_lines: But he played ball with the tuskers,
Turned the steeds to cotton,
Bore the sword-points of the vile upon his chest,
Leaving his beloved to suffer as time moves on,
Leaving this old woman too floating in tears,
He finished his duty.
notes: `களிறுகளை பந்தாடி` remains the violent `played ball with the tuskers` image.
The verified `புரவிகளை பஞ்சாக்கி` is translated conservatively as `turned the steeds to cotton`; it is not silently replaced with a familiar martial cliché.

source_tamil_lines: களிப்பொரு பக்கம் கண்ணில் நீர் ஒரு பக்கம்
english_lines: Joy on one side, water in the eye on one side,
I praise the son who won fame on the battlefield,
Am I not the mother who bore him in the womb?
That is why I wither,
(My two eyes).
notes: `களப்புகழ்` remains battlefield fame, and the final womb/mother line keeps the song's simultaneous public pride and private grief.

translator_notes: The song's mother-warrior voice is retained without sentimental smoothing: pride, battlefield violence, the planned marriage, the abandoned lover and maternal grief remain in the same rhetorical frame.
This is a literary source-faithful translation, not a singable adaptation.
